items.label: Data Types — uint, bool, string, address

slides.title: Revision — What We Learned in Lecture 1
slides.definition: Before diving deeper into Solidity programming, let us quickly revise the key foundations from Lecture 1 that this entire lecture builds upon.
keyPoints: Blockchain — distributed, decentralized, tamper-proof ledger shared across thousands of nodes worldwide
Ethereum — a programmable blockchain; a 'world computer' that runs smart contracts using the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine)
Smart Contracts — programs deployed to the blockchain at a fixed address; immutable, automatic, trustless — no human intermediary needed
MetaMask — browser wallet for managing your Ethereum account (private key, public address, ETH balance) and signing transactions
Remix IDE — browser-based development environment; write, compile, deploy, and test Solidity contracts with zero installation
First Solidity Contract — we wrote a simple storage contract; learned pragma solidity, contract keyword, and state variables

slides.title: Solidity Syntax Basics
slides.definition: Solidity syntax is heavily influenced by JavaScript and C++. Every .sol file must begin with two mandatory declarations: an SPDX license identifier and a pragma version directive. Without these, the compiler will issue warnings or errors.
keyPoints: // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT — declares the open-source license for your code; MIT is the most permissive; required on every file to suppress compiler warnings
pragma solidity ^0.8.20; — tells the compiler which version to use; ^ means 'this version or any compatible patch version but NOT the next major version (0.9.x)'
Solidity 0.8.x is recommended for all new contracts — built-in overflow and underflow protection replaces the old SafeMath library pattern
contract Variables { } — the contract keyword is like a class in OOP; it wraps all your state and logic
Solidity is statically typed — every variable must declare its type explicitly before use (unlike JavaScript which is dynamic)
Semicolons ; are mandatory at end of every statement — forgetting one is a very common beginner compile error

slides.title: Data Types Overview — The Building Blocks
leftItems: uint — unsigned integer; cannot be negative; most common type in Solidity; default is uint256
int — signed integer; can hold negative values; default is int256
bool — boolean; only true or false; 1 byte of storage
address — 20-byte Ethereum address; holds wallet or contract addresses; one of the most unique types in Solidity
bytes32 — fixed-size 32-byte array; efficient for short data like IDs, hashes, roles
bytes1 to bytes32 — fixed-size byte arrays for raw binary data
enum — user-defined named constants; stored as uint8 internally (e.g. Status.Active = 0)
rightItems: string — dynamic UTF-8 encoded text; stored as a dynamic bytes array; expensive on-chain
bytes — dynamic raw byte array; more gas-efficient than string for non-text binary data
uint256[] — dynamic array; can grow and shrink; supports .push() and .pop()
uint256[5] — fixed-size array; size is hardcoded at compile time; cannot change
mapping(key => value) — hash table; the most widely used data structure in Solidity
struct — groups related variables into a single named type (like a record or object)
Reference types MUST declare their data location: storage, memory, or calldata

slides.title: uint — Unsigned Integer (Most Used Type)
slides.definition: uint (unsigned integer) can only store zero and positive whole numbers. It cannot store decimals or negative numbers. In Solidity, uint is an alias for uint256 — a 256-bit number ranging from 0 to 2^256 - 1 (a number with 77 digits).
keyPoints: Other sizes: uint8 (0-255), uint16 (0-65535), uint32, uint64, uint128 — use smaller sizes to pack structs and save gas
Example: uint public age = 25; — valid. uint public temp = -5; — COMPILE ERROR (negative not allowed)
uint is used for: token balances, prices, timestamps (block.timestamp is uint256), counters, IDs, percentages
Solidity 0.8.x: if uint overflows (goes above max) the transaction automatically REVERTS — no silent wrapping bug
Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % (modulus), ** (exponentiation) — all supported natively
Gas tip: uint256 is actually the cheapest to use on the EVM — the EVM word size is 256 bits, so smaller uints cost extra conversion ops

slides.title: bool, string & address Types
leftItems: Stores only: true or false
Default value if uninitialized: false
Example: bool public isActive = true;
Real use cases: user verified status, NFT minted flag, transaction completed marker, contract paused state
Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT)
Comparison: == (equals), != (not equals)
Common pattern: require(isActive, 'Contract is paused') — gate functions with bool flags
rightItems: string public name = "Ali"; — stores UTF-8 text; dynamic size; expensive in storage
Cannot compare strings directly with ==; use keccak256(abi.encodePacked(s1)) == keccak256(abi.encodePacked(s2))
address public owner; — stores a 20-byte Ethereum address starting with 0x
address payable — a special address that can receive ETH (has .transfer() and .send() methods)
address(0) — the zero address 0x0000...0000; used as 'null' equivalent; tokens sent here are burned
msg.sender — a global variable of type address; always equals the caller of the function
address.balance — returns ETH balance of any address in wei (uint256)

slides.title: State Variables vs Local Variables
leftItems: Declared INSIDE the contract but OUTSIDE any function
Stored permanently on the blockchain in contract storage (key-value store)
Persist between function calls — their value is remembered forever
Reading costs 2,100 gas (cold) or 100 gas (warm); writing costs 20,000 gas (new) or 5,000 gas (update)
Example: uint public age = 25; — exists in storage slot 0 of the contract
public keyword auto-generates a free getter function — age() can be called externally with no gas
Uninitialized state variables get default values: uint = 0, bool = false, address = 0x000...000
rightItems: Declared INSIDE a function body — only exist during that function's execution
Stored in memory (or on the EVM stack for value types) — FREE, no gas cost for storage
Destroyed completely when the function finishes — not persisted anywhere
Example: uint number = 10; inside a function — exists only during that call
Value types (uint, bool, address) go on the EVM stack automatically
Reference types (string, arrays, structs) inside functions must use memory keyword
Rule of thumb: if the variable needs to survive after the function ends, make it a state variable

slides.title: Default Values — Solidity Initializes Everything
slides.definition: In Solidity, you never have null or undefined. Every uninitialized variable automatically receives a default (zero) value based on its type. This is a key safety feature that prevents many bugs common in other languages.
keyPoints: uint / int → 0 (zero)
bool → false
string → "" (empty string)
Dynamic arrays → [] (empty array with length 0)
Practical importance: mapping(address => uint) balances — if you query an address that never deposited, it returns 0 automatically, not an error

slides.title: Storage, Memory & Calldata
slides.subtitle: The Most Important Gas Optimization Concept in Solidity
slides.description: Solidity requires you to explicitly declare WHERE data lives. This is unlike most languages. Each location has different cost, lifetime, and mutability rules. Getting this wrong causes either compilation errors or expensive unnecessary gas usage.

properties.desc: Permanent blockchain data. Persists forever. Most expensive: SSTORE costs 20,000 gas (new slot) or 5,000 gas (update). All state variables live here automatically.
Temporary — exists only during function execution. Cheap: ~3 gas per byte. Must declare for reference types (strings, arrays, structs) inside functions. Erased after call.
Read-only external input. Cheapest option for function parameters in external functions. Cannot be modified. Use for string and bytes parameters you only need to read.
State that persists → storage (automatic). Temp computation inside function → memory. External function input you won't modify → calldata (saves gas).

slides.example: function greet(string calldata _name) external pure returns (string memory) — calldata for input (read-only, cheap), memory for output (temp return value)

slides.title: Functions — Defining Smart Contract Behavior
slides.definition: Functions are the executable units of a smart contract. They define what the contract CAN DO. Every interaction with a deployed contract — reading data, writing data, transferring ETH — goes through a function call.
keyPoints: Syntax: function functionName(paramType paramName) visibility modifier returns(returnType) { body }
function add(uint a, uint b) public pure returns(uint) { return a + b; } — complete example
Parameters: type comes first, then name — e.g. uint a, bool flag, address user
Multiple return values: returns(uint, bool) — Solidity supports tuple returns natively
Named returns: returns(uint result) — you can assign to result and return; without explicit return keyword
Functions that modify state cost gas; functions that only read state are free when called off-chain (view/pure)
Fallback function: receive() external payable — called when ETH is sent to contract with no data

slides.title: Function Visibility — Who Can Call What
leftItems: public — callable from ANYWHERE: inside the same contract, from child contracts, and from external wallets/contracts. Auto-generates a getter for state variables.
private — ONLY callable from within the exact same contract. NOT inherited by child contracts. Most restrictive.
internal — callable from within the contract AND from any child (derived) contract that inherits it. NOT externally callable.
external — ONLY callable from outside the contract (other contracts or wallets). Cannot be called internally with functionName() — must use this.functionName(). Most gas-efficient for large inputs.
rightItems: uint private secret = 100; — state variable private: no auto-getter, no external access
function getSecret() public view returns(uint) { return secret; } — public function exposes private data in a controlled way
internal functions are the foundation of inheritance — OpenZeppelin uses them extensively
external + calldata is the cheapest combination for functions receiving large string or bytes arguments
Default visibility for functions in older Solidity was public — in 0.8.x you MUST declare it explicitly or get a compile error
Rule: start everything as private/internal; only open up to public/external what needs to be accessible
Security: private does NOT mean secret — all blockchain data is readable. It only restricts which code can call it.

slides.title: view vs pure — Reading the Blockchain
leftItems: view means: this function READS state but does NOT modify it
Can access: state variables, block.timestamp, msg.sender, other view functions
FREE to call if called externally (off-chain by a wallet or dApp) — zero gas
Costs gas if called internally from a state-changing function (because it's part of a transaction)
Example: function getOwner() public view returns(address) { return owner; }
Example: function getBalance(address user) public view returns(uint) { return balances[user]; }
Compiler enforces: if a view function accidentally writes state, you get a compile error
rightItems: pure means: function NEITHER reads NOR modifies any blockchain state
Cannot access: state variables, block.timestamp, msg.sender — nothing from the chain
Entirely self-contained mathematical or utility functions
FREE to call externally — pure functions are essentially off-chain computation
Example: function add(uint a, uint b) public pure returns(uint) { return a + b; }
Example: function percentage(uint amount, uint pct) public pure returns(uint) { return (amount * pct) / 100; }
Compiler enforces: if a pure function reads state, you get a compile error. Use pure as documentation + safety.

slides.title: Constructor & msg.sender
slides.definition: The constructor is a special function that runs EXACTLY ONCE — during contract deployment. It is used to set the initial state of the contract. msg.sender is a global Solidity variable that always holds the address of whoever sent the current transaction or call.
keyPoints: constructor() { } — no function keyword, no visibility specifier needed in Solidity 0.8.x
Runs at deployment time only — can never be called again after the contract is on-chain
Most common use: setting the contract owner — address public owner; constructor() { owner = msg.sender; }
msg.sender during constructor = the wallet address that deployed the contract (the deployer)
msg.sender during a normal function call = whoever called that function (could be a user or another contract)
msg.value — the amount of ETH (in wei) sent with the transaction; only accessible in payable functions
onlyOwner pattern: modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, 'Not owner'); _; } — most common access control in Solidity

slides.title: Common Beginner Mistakes in Solidity
slides.intro: These mistakes are made by almost every student in their first week of Solidity. Knowing them in advance will save you hours of debugging. The Solidity compiler catches some but not all of these.
bullets: MISTAKE 1 — Forgetting memory keyword on reference types: function test(string name) → COMPILE ERROR. Correct: function test(string memory name). Applies to string, bytes, arrays, structs in function parameters

MISTAKE 2 — Using view when the function modifies state: marking a function view but using assignment (=) or .push() inside it. Compiler catches this — 'Function declared as view, but this expression (potentially) modifies the state'

MISTAKE 3 — Thinking private means secret: private only prevents OTHER contracts from calling your function. ALL data in contract storage is publicly readable by anyone who queries the blockchain directly
MISTAKE 4 — Integer division truncates: 5 / 2 = 2 in Solidity, not 2.5. Solidity has no floating point. Multiply before dividing: (amount * percentage) / 100, not amount / 100 * percentage

MISTAKE 5 — msg.sender in a pure function: pure functions have no access to global variables. If you need msg.sender, use view or no modifier (state-changing). Compiler error: 'Function cannot be declared as pure'
MISTAKE 6 — Accessing mapping with non-existent key expecting an error: Solidity silently returns the default value (0, false, address(0)) — no KeyError. You must validate separately with require()

slides.title: Practical — Student Registry Smart Contract
leftItems: // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;
contract StudentRegistry {
struct Student { string name; uint age; }
Student[] public students;
function addStudent(string memory _name, uint _age) public { students.push(Student(_name, _age)); }
function getStudentsCount() public view returns(uint) { return students.length; }
rightItems: struct — groups name (string) and age (uint) into one Student type; analogous to a row in a database table
Student[] public students — a dynamic array of Student structs stored permanently in contract storage
string memory _name — parameter uses memory because string is a reference type; underscore prefix is convention for parameters
students.push(Student(_name, _age)) — creates a new Student struct inline and appends it to the array
students.length — built-in property of all arrays; returns current count as uint
public view returns(uint) — getStudentsCount reads state, returns nothing on-chain, zero gas for external calls
Test in Remix: addStudent('Ali', 20) then addStudent('Sara', 22) then call getStudentsCount() — should return 2

categories.uses: Create contract MyProfile. Store: name (string), age (uint), city (string). Add getter functions for each. Deploy and test in Remix.
Create Calculator with: add(uint a, uint b), subtract, multiply, divide, modulus. All pure functions. Test all operations in Remix.
Store a struct Task { string title; bool completed; }. Dynamic array of Tasks. addTask(string memory _title). markComplete(uint index).
Extend StudentRegistry: add updateStudent(uint index, string memory _name, uint _age), deleteStudent(uint index), mapping(address => uint) studentCount per address.
Add constructor that sets owner = msg.sender. Create modifier onlyOwner(). Restrict addStudent to onlyOwner. Test: non-owner call should revert.
Use Remix debugger to step through addStudent transaction. Inspect: stack, memory, storage slots. Use Remix Gas Profiler to compare view vs state-changing calls.

slides.title: Important Questions — Test Your Understanding
leftItems: Q1: What is the difference between storage and memory? Which is permanent and which is temporary? Which costs more gas?
Q2: What is the difference between view and pure? Can a view function modify state? Can a pure function read msg.sender?
Q3: What is msg.sender? What does it return when a contract calls another contract?
Q4: Why do we use uint instead of int for most counters, balances, and IDs in Solidity?
Q5: What is the difference between a state variable and a local variable? Where is each stored?
rightItems: Q6: What is wrong with this? function test(string name) public pure returns(string) { return name; }
Q7: What visibility modifier allows child contracts to call a function but blocks external callers?
Q8: What is the default value of an uninitialized address variable in Solidity?
Q9: How many times does the constructor run? When exactly does it run?
Q10: You have mapping(address => uint) public balances. User 0xABC never deposited. What does balances[0xABC] return?
Q11: Why is 7 / 2 = 3 in Solidity and not 3.5? How do you handle decimal math in Solidity?
Q12: What does the public keyword do when applied to a state variable like uint public age = 25?

slides.title: Helpful Resources & Tools
slides.definition: These are the official, most reliable resources for Solidity development. Bookmark all of them. The Solidity documentation is your primary reference — most answers to syntax questions are there.
keyPoints: Solidity Official Docs — docs.soliditylang.org — full language reference, examples, security patterns; version-specific docs available for every release
Remix IDE — remix.ethereum.org — browser-based; no installation; supports compile, deploy, debug, gas profiling; perfect for all lecture practicals
OpenZeppelin Contracts — docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts — audited, production-ready base contracts; ERC-20, ERC-721, Ownable, AccessControl — never write these from scratch
Ethereum Official — ethereum.org/developers — tutorials, developer guides, EIP specifications, Solidity by Example
Alchemy Sepolia Faucet — sepoliafaucet.com — get free Sepolia testnet ETH for deploying contracts; requires an Alchemy account
Etherscan Sepolia — sepolia.etherscan.io — explore your deployed test contracts, verify source code, inspect transactions and events

slides.title: Lecture #2 Summary — Key Takeaways
points: Every Solidity file must start with SPDX license identifier and pragma solidity version — these are mandatory, not optional
Solidity is statically typed: uint, int, bool, string, address, bytes32 — every variable must declare its type explicitly before use
State variables live permanently in blockchain storage; local variables live temporarily in memory during a single function call
Three data locations: storage (permanent, expensive), memory (temporary, cheap), calldata (read-only, cheapest) — use the right one or pay unnecessary gas
Four visibility levels: public (everyone), private (same contract only), internal (contract + children), external (outside only) — default to private, open up only what must be accessible
view reads state without changing it (free externally); pure neither reads nor changes state (free externally); both are enforced by the compiler
Constructor runs exactly once at deployment — use it to set owner = msg.sender and initialize critical state
You can now build real smart contracts: Student Registry, Calculator, Todo List — deploy these on Remix and Sepolia testnet for practice
slides.closing: Master these fundamentals and every advanced Solidity concept — ERC-20, NFTs, DeFi — becomes a natural extension.
